2329666.title: Cabinet approves Rs 10,000 Crore Scheme to Make India a Global Container Manufacturing Hub
2329666.ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
2329666.body_html:
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
Cabinet approves Rs 10,000 Crore Scheme to Make India a Global Container Manufacturing Hub
Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme to raise domestic capacity ten-fold to 7.5 lakh TEUs and strengthen India's maritime supply chain
Sonowal thanks PM Modi for Make in India push: A strong step to reduce import dependence and secure our logistics chain
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 6:09PM by PIB Delhi

The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, today approved the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme (CMPS), a Rs 10,000 crore programme announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 to build a globally competitive container manufacturing ecosystem in India. The scheme will run from FY 2027-28 to FY 2039-40, with three years for setting up facilities and ten years of production support.

The scheme will support new factories as well as the expansion of existing units. It aims to lift India's annual container manufacturing capacity around ten-fold, to 7.5 lakh TEUs, from about 70,000 TEUs today. Union Minister of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPSW), Sarbananda Sonowal welcomed this announcement by thanking Prime Minister Narendra Modi for emboldening Make In India push in container manufacturing in the country.

"I express my heartfelt gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his visionary leadership. His Make in India push is giving our container manufacturers the confidence to build at scale, and this scheme is a strong step to reduce import dependence," Sarbananda Sonowal said.

India's trade depends on containers, but almost all of them are made abroad. India's container traffic is projected to grow from about 24 million TEUs in 2024 to 175 million TEUs by 2047 under the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision, which makes home-grown capacity critical.

What the scheme offers

  • Interest Subvention Assistance (Rs 859 crore): 3 per cent a year on eligible term loans for greenfield plants of at least 1,00,000 TEUs a year and brownfield expansions of at least 25,000 TEUs a year.
  • Operational Expenditure Assistance (Rs 8,891 crore): support for every container made to global shipping standards and sold by an eligible manufacturer, to bridge the cost gap with imports. Domestic content must rise from 70 per cent to 90 per cent.
  • Testing and Certification (Rs 150 crore): common facilities, such as dynamic longitudinal impact testing, to reduce dependence on overseas testing.
  • Scheme management (Rs 100 crore): administration, monitoring and capacity building.
  • Land at major ports: leasing support at 25 per cent of the notified rate.

An Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, will approve guidelines and sanction assistance.

The scheme is expected to create about 3,000 direct and more than 50,000 indirect jobs, in steel, components and logistics. It will also support ancillary industries such as corner castings, specialised steel, wooden frames and paints. The government estimates it will generate about Rs 75,000 crore of economic output by FY 2039-40, more than seven times the support provided. Demand is expected from replacement of the global fleet, the Bharat Container Shipping Line, and new mega ports such as Vadhavan and Galathea Bay.

"Containers are the backbone of our trade. By making them in India, we strengthen the maritime logistics supply chain on which our ports, our exporters and our shipping lines depend, and we take another step towards a self-reliant India and the goals of Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047," Sonowal added.

2329660.title: MCA’s cleanliness drive ‘Special campaign 6.0’ yield impressive revenue of Rs. 10,50,520 through e-waste management, recycling initiatives
2329660.body_html:
Ministry of Corporate Affairs
MCA’s cleanliness drive ‘Special campaign 6.0’ yield impressive revenue of Rs. 10,50,520 through e-waste management, recycling initiatives
MCA successfully addresses public grievances, resolving 316 out of 330 pending CPGRAMs, clear 217 public grievances out of 435 pending appeals
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 6:03PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) has successfully driven significant operational efficiency, cleanliness, and record management milestones under the ongoing Special Campaign 6.0. Demonstrating a strong commitment to institutional excellence and environmental responsibility, the Ministry recorded remarkable outcomes across multiple key performance indicators.

As part of the nationwide cleanliness drive, all 75 planned cleanliness campaigns were successfully conducted well before time. This year, the Ministry has exceeded its initial projections by initiating additional drives. This proactive approach resulted in freeing up of 15,740 square feet of office space and projections are that more space will be opened up as the clean-up continues.

Furthermore, the campaign yielded an impressive revenue of Rs. 10,50,520 through e-waste management and recycling initiatives, successfully processing electronic and electrical equipment.

In the domain of record management and grievance redressal, the Ministry made rapid progress by weeding out 850 files out of identified 2,523 physical files for weeding, alongside reviewing 8,823 physical files out of 9,309 target files. Additionally, the administration successfully addressed public grievances, resolving 316 out of 330 pending CPGRAMs, and cleared 217 public grievance appeals out of 435 pending appeals.

Parliamentary and PMO reference targets are also being systematically monitored to ensure timely administrative action.

These achievements underscore that the Ministry is dedicated to fostering a transparent, accountable, and citizen-centric governance framework by promoting sustainable e-waste recycling, reclaiming valuable office space, and accelerating administrative responsiveness.

2329624.title: Indian Culinary Institute Signs MoU with Jawaharlal Nehru University for Recognition of BBA and MBA Programmes
2329624.body_html:
Ministry of Tourism
Indian Culinary Institute Signs MoU with Jawaharlal Nehru University for Recognition of BBA and MBA Programmes
MoU to enable award of degrees by JNU to students completing BBA and MBA programmes at Indian Culinary Institute
Collaboration to enhance higher education and employment opportunities for students in India and abroad
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 5:43PM by PIB Delhi

The Indian Culinary Institute (ICI), an institute under the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), New Delhi, today at Kartavya Bhawan, New Delhi. The MoU was signed by Smt. Santishree Dhulipudi Pandit, Vice-Chancellor, JNU, and Shri Gyan Bhushan, Director, ICI, on behalf of their respective institutions, in the presence of Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Union Minister for Tourism and Culture, and Shri Bhuvnesh Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Tourism. Senior officials from the Ministry of Tourism, JNU and ICI were also present on the occasion.

The MoU provides for the recognition of ICI’s BBA (Culinary Arts & Food Business) and MBA (Culinary Management) programmes by JNU, enabling the university to award degrees to students successfully completing these programmes at ICI.

The BBA and MBA programmes offered by ICI aim to develop highly skilled chefs and hospitality professionals to meet the growing requirements of the hotel, hospitality and allied industries. The programmes focus on equipping students with the requisite skills, knowledge and professional competencies to excel in the hospitality sector. They also seek to nurture culinary professionals who contribute to the distinct identity and offerings of hotels and restaurants.

The recognition of ICI’s BBA and MBA programmes by JNU, commencing from the next academic year, is expected to enhance academic and professional opportunities for students. The collaboration will facilitate access to higher education and improve employment and placement prospects for graduates, both in India and abroad, while contributing to the growing demand for skilled professionals in India’s hospitality sector.

2329609.title: From Financial Barriers To Global Innovation:  A Journey Of Ambition And Opportunity
2329609.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Financial Barriers To Global Innovation: A Journey Of Ambition And Opportunity
National Overseas Scholarship Enables SC Student to Pursue Higher Education at Brown University, USA
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 5:31PM by PIB Delhi

Growing up in a middle-class Scheduled Caste family, Aarav Patel (name changed) aspired to build a career at the intersection of technology, business and innovation.

He envisioned establishing successful technology-driven enterprises and making a meaningful contribution to society through his work. However, limited financial resources, inadequate mentorship and a lack of professional networks in advanced science and engineering careers presented significant challenges.

The high cost of pursuing quality higher education at leading international universities posed a major financial barrier. In addition, limited access to experienced mentors and professional networks made it difficult to navigate advanced academic opportunities and understand potential career pathways in science and engineering. Despite these constraints, he remained committed to acquiring the knowledge, skills and global exposure necessary to pursue his ambitions.

The National Overseas Scholarship (NOS) Scheme provided crucial financial assistance, enabling him to pursue a Master of Science (MSc) degree at Brown University in the United States. During the financial year 2023–24, assistance amounting to US$ 89,816 was provided, with support approved on 26 June 2023. The assistance covered tuition fees, maintenance allowance, visa fees, medical insurance and travel expenses.

By addressing the substantial financial requirements associated with overseas education, the scheme helped the beneficiary access an advanced academic environment and acquire specialised knowledge, skills and credentials relevant to his professional aspirations. His international educational experience strengthened his understanding of technology, innovation and business development.

Today, the beneficiary is a business owner and director, working towards his ambition of building successful technology-driven enterprises. The qualification and exposure gained through his studies have provided him with a stronger foundation to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities. His family continues to belong to the middle-income segment, while the educational opportunity has expanded his professional horizons and equipped him with capabilities to pursue future growth.

The National Overseas Scholarship Scheme reflects the Government of India's commitment to expanding access to higher education for eligible students from Scheduled Castes and other specified categories, in accordance with the scheme's guidelines. By supporting tuition and other essential expenses associated with overseas study, the scheme helps eligible students access international academic institutions, strengthen their professional capabilities and pursue their aspirations.

The beneficiary's journey demonstrates how targeted educational assistance can help bridge financial barriers, widen access to global learning opportunities and nurture the aspirations of future professionals and entrepreneurs. From overcoming financial constraints to pursuing global education and entrepreneurship, his story highlights the transformative potential of educational opportunity in building a foundation for innovation, ambition and social progress.

2329583.title: Government Facilitating Startup-Industry Linkages to Take Indigenous Innovations to the Market, says Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh
2329583.body_html:
Ministry of Science & Technology
Government Facilitating Startup-Industry Linkages to Take Indigenous Innovations to the Market, says Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh
Dr Jitendra Singh visits the exhibition at ESTIC 2026, featuring selected 50 deep-tech startups, 13 departmental stalls and 10 departmental technologies, reflecting the breadth of India’s scientific and technological capabilities
ESTIC-2026 Provides a Platform for Startups, Scientific Institutions and Industry to Explore Collaboration: Dr. Jitendra Singh
Indigenous Technologies Reflect India’s Growing Scientific and Technological Capabilities, says the Union Minister
Modi Govt Focused on Connecting Innovation with Practical Applications and Wider Adoption: Dr. Jitendra Singh
Dr. Jitendra Singh Urges Stakeholders to Leverage Opportunities to Strengthen India’s Innovation Ecosystem
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 5:15PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and Minister of State for PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, has called for stronger linkages between StartUps and industry, emphasising the Government’s role in facilitating partnerships that can help indigenous innovations move from research and development to wider commercial adoption.

The Minister said that India’s expanding innovation ecosystem offers significant opportunities for startups to connect with industry and other potential technology adopters, develop practical applications and scale up their solutions. He urged stakeholders to come forward and make effective use of these opportunities to strengthen India’s innovation-led growth.

Dr. Jitendra Singh visited the exhibition of StartUps, scientific institutions and departmental technologies at the 'Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave' (ESTIC)-2026, being held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from October 27 to 29.

The conclave features selected 50 deep-tech startups, 13 departmental stalls and 10 departmental technologies, reflecting the breadth of India’s scientific and technological capabilities.

During his visit, the Minister reviewed a range of innovations demonstrating how scientific research is addressing challenges across sectors, from food and nutrition to advanced electronics. Among the exhibits was CSIR Designer Rice, a high-protein, low-glycaemic-index rice developed at CSIR–National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology (CSIR-NIIST).

The rice contains approximately 20 per cent protein and has a reported glycaemic index of 54, placing it in the low-GI category. Developed using rice fractions and structural modification, the innovation represents an effort to create food products with improved nutritional characteristics and potential relevance for people seeking better dietary management.

The exhibition also showcased JEET, the SCMC4212 microcontroller unit developed by Signalchip, reflecting India's growing capabilities in indigenous semiconductor and electronic-system design. Powered by a Yati 32-bit RISC-V CPU and an Avarta 32-bit digital signal processor, the microcontroller integrates memory, power-management and other functional capabilities in a compact design. Its potential applications include flight controllers, Internet of Things devices, smart devices, robotics and industrial automation. Such home-grown technologies can contribute to the development of domestic capabilities in strategic and emerging technology domains.

Other displays included bio-based packaging and reusable or application-specific products, illustrating the wider scope of innovation in materials and sustainability. Together, the exhibits demonstrate how India's scientific institutions, entrepreneurs and technology developers are working across diverse fields to develop solutions with practical applications, while creating opportunities for technology partnerships and commercial deployment.

Dr. Jitendra Singh has consistently advocated stronger coordination among research institutions, startups, industry and government to ensure that scientific discoveries translate into tangible economic and societal benefits. The exhibition at ESTIC-2026 provides an opportunity for startups to engage directly with prospective partners, identify applications for their technologies and explore pathways for scaling up their innovations.

The Minister urged industry leaders, investors, research institutions and other stakeholders to actively engage with startups and indigenous technology developers, build mutually beneficial partnerships and help take promising Indian innovations to wider markets. Stronger collaboration across the innovation ecosystem, he said, can help accelerate technology adoption, strengthen domestic technological capabilities and advance the national vision of Viksit Bharat@2047.

2329565.title: From Substance Dependence To Self-Reliance Karim Nagar Telangana’s Neel’s Journey Of Recovery
2329565.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Substance Dependence To Self-Reliance Karim Nagar Telangana’s Neel’s Journey Of Recovery
Rehabilitation Support through the Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 5:01PM by PIB Delhi

Recovery from substance dependence help individuals rebuild their health, relationships and economic stability.

The journey of NEEL (name changed), a 25-year-old graduate from Karimnagar, Telangana, highlights the role of comprehensive rehabilitation and continued support in helping individuals work towards a healthier and more stable life.

NEEL began consuming alcohol and cannabis due to peer influence and family stress. Over time, substance use affected his work performance, health and family relationships. He experienced financial instability, social isolation, emotional disconnection and declining confidence. His family was also affected financially and emotionally, but continued to support him through treatment and rehabilitation.

On 22 May 2026, NEEL received support through the Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA) at Prakriti Environment Society in Karimnagar, Telangana. The assistance included medical treatment, detoxification, individual counselling, behavioural therapy, emotional and psychological support, and family counselling.

Vocational guidance, follow-up care and relapse prevention services further supported his recovery and helped him work towards rebuilding his personal and professional life.

Family motivation and comprehensive rehabilitation support helped NEEL develop healthier habits, strengthen family relationships and regain confidence. The combination of counselling, treatment and continued care supported his efforts to maintain sobriety and move towards a more stable and independent future.

Today, NEEL is maintaining sobriety, working regularly and earning approximately Rs 15,000 per month. His regular income has enabled him to contribute to his family’s well-being, while improved relationships and renewed confidence have helped him move forward with greater stability.

NEEL’s journey demonstrates the importance of accessible treatment, professional counselling, family participation and sustained follow-up care in supporting recovery from substance dependence.

The rehabilitation services provided through the IRCA at Prakriti Environment Society highlight how comprehensive support can help individuals rebuild their lives, restore family relationships and work towards social and economic reintegration.

Indian Naval Ship Sahyadri, an indigenously designed and built guided missile stealth frigate of the Indian Navy, arrived at Busan Naval Harbour, Republic of Korea, on 26 Oct 2026 to participate in the India-Republic of Korea Navy (IN-RoKN) Bilateral Exercise. During the harbour phase, personnel of both navies will participate in professional interactions, cross-deck visits, cross-training activities and sporting events. These activities will facilitate the exchange of operational experiences and Best Practices, while fostering mutual understanding and professional camaraderie. The Commanding Officer of INS Sahyadri will also call on senior RoKN officials. The harbour phase will be followed by coordinated maritime activities at sea involving INS Sahyadri and ROKS Munmu the Great, providing opportunities to strengthen operational coordination, enhance interoperability and consolidate professional ties between the two navies.

The exercise underscores the shared commitment of India and the Republic of Korea to strengthening maritime cooperation and contributing to peace, stability and security in the Indo-Pacific. It also reflects the Indian Navy’s continued efforts to build enduring partnerships with friendly foreign navies through professional engagement and operational cooperation.

2329561.title: TRAI Assesses Mobile Network Quality Across Gonda, Bahraich, Shravasti & Balrampur City, Prayagraj to Gonda and Gonda to Bahraich Highway under UPE LSA, during the month of September 2026
2329561.body_html:
Ministry of Communications
TRAI Assesses Mobile Network Quality Across Gonda, Bahraich, Shravasti & Balrampur City, Prayagraj to Gonda and Gonda to Bahraich Highway under UPE LSA, during the month of September 2026
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 4:53PM by PIB Delhi

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has released findings of Independent Drive Test (IDT) conducted through its appointed agency across Gonda, Bahraich, Shravasti and Balrampur City under UPE LSA, during the month of September 2026, for information of general telecom consumers. The purpose of this drive test is to assess and verify real time quality of mobile network services (both voice & data) provided by Telecom Service Providers (TSPs). The performance of TSPs for key Quality of Service (QoS) parameters, captured during IDT are published to inform Consumers and encourage TSPs to improve their services. These IDTs have been designed to capture on ground mobile network performance of all TSPs across diverse usages environment like cities, hotspots, public transport hubs, etc.

These tests were conducted under the supervision of the TRAI Regional Office Bhopal. The observations presented in drive test reports represent the performance of the TSPs on the area/ route under test on the day/ time of conducting the drive test.

The drive tests conducted across City drive – 367.7 KMs in Gonda, Bahraich, Shravasti and Balrampur and 2.7 Km walk Test in Gonda & Balrampur City and 256 KMs Highway drive from Prayagraj to Gonda and Gonda to Bahraich, from 7th September 2026 to 10th September 2026 in UPE LSA.

Drive Test Route Map: The following map provides overview of drive test routes indicating City drive, Inter-operator calling, Hotspots and Walk tests, as per the legends shown on the map: -

Key Parameters Assessed

  1. Coverage Gap: Percentage of samples, for which signal strength observed less than the minimum prescribed signal strength for respective technology (2G/ 3G/ 4G/ 5G).
  2. Voice Services: Call Setup Success Rate (CSSR), Drop Call Rate (DCR), Call Setup Time, Call Silence (Mute) Rate, Speech Quality (MOS).

2329363.bureau: PIB Delhi The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has extended the last date for media accreditation for the
2329363.body_html:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
MIB Extends IFFI 2026 Media Accreditation Deadline till 4th November 2026
Film Enthusiasts can also Register as Delegates to Experience a New World of Cinema
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 12:37PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has extended the last date for media accreditation for the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026 till 4th November 2026.

Media professionals planning to cover the festival, scheduled to be held in Panaji, Goa, from 20th to 28th November 2026, can submit their applications through the official Press Information Bureau (PIB) accreditation portal.

Eligible media persons are advised to complete their registration and upload the required documents before the revised deadline.

Registration Link: https://accreditation.pib.gov.in/eventregistration/login.aspx

For queries, applicants may contact iffi.mediadesk@pib.gov.in.

Accredited media professionals will have access to various festival activities, including:

•           Film screenings

•           Panel discussions

•           Interactions with filmmakers and cinema professionals

•           Networking opportunities

•           Other activities related to festival coverage

Media professionals who are already registered on the portal for previous edition (56th) of IFFI, can use the same credentials to log in and update their documents as required.

Apply early to secure your place at one of Asia’s most celebrated film festivals, connect with voices shaping the world of cinema, discover stories beyond the screen and be part of IFFI’s vibrant celebration of filmmaking, creativity and culture.

Furthermore, film enthusiasts who are not media persons may also register for IFFI as Delegates vide https://www.iffigoa.org/delegate-registration and enjoy the rich tapestry of films and other activities on offer at 57th IFFI 2026.

 

About IFFI

Born in 1952, the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) is South Asia’s oldest and largest celebration of cinema. Jointly hosted by the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC), Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India and the Entertainment Society of Goa (ESG), State Government of Goa, IFFI brings together filmmakers, legends and emerging voices from across the world. With international competitions, cultural showcases, masterclasses and tributes, the festival celebrates diverse stories, languages and cinematic traditions against the vibrant backdrop of Goa.

For more information and latest details about the 57th IFFI 2026 please visit https://www.iffigoa.org/.

****

2329355.title: India's New-Age Space Technologies
2329355.body_html:
PIB Backgrounder
India's New-Age Space Technologies
The Road to Self-Reliance
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 12:19PM by PIB Delhi

India’s space journey began in 1963 with a sounding rocket launched from Thumba, Kerala. It now looks ahead to the planned Bharatiya Antariksh Station. New technologies are driving this progress. They include reusable launch vehicles, electric, green and nuclear propulsion, and in-orbit servicing. Through SpaDeX, India also became the fourth country to achieve autonomous docking of two spacecraft in orbit. These advances strengthen self-reliance. Meanwhile, Gaganyaan is advancing India’s human spaceflight goals.

Space Science & Relevance for Today

India’s organised space activities began in 1962 with the establishment of the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) under the vision of Dr Vikram A. Sarabhai. The first sounding rocket was launched from Thumba, Kerala on 21 November 1963. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed on 15 August 1969, superseding INCOSPAR, and was subsequently brought under the Department of Space in 1972. Since its inception, ISRO followed a development-first philosophy: using space technology to solve problems on the ground. Over the decades, it grew far beyond a launch service provider, and its efficiency and technical excellence have earned global recognition. That reputation now rests on a simple promise: every mission must serve the common citizen.

That vision now shapes daily life across the country. Communication satellites extend connectivity to remote and underserved areas. Earth observation data support agriculture, disaster assessment, planning, environmental monitoring and other national requirements. Weather satellites track cyclones and monsoons, enabling early warnings that save lives. Fishermen, farmers and coastal communities rely on these alerts to protect their livelihoods. These systems connect citizens, protect communities, strengthen governance and drive inclusive, sustainable growth. Beyond these services, space also guards India’s frontiers and shapes its future. Space-based communication systems support national security and strategic requirements.

Building on these strengths, emerging technologies are opening fresh avenues for innovation, connectivity and service delivery. Private enterprises and start-ups are now joining this journey. This positions India as a confident, self-reliant and globally respected space power. Click To Read More in Detail: India's Space Odyssey

 

Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies

ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India's Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave. ESTIC 2026 is being scheduled for 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The Space Science & Technologies thematic session, organised by the Department of Space/ISRO on 29 October 2026, is one of the conclave’s thematic programmes. Read More on Agenda: ESTIC 2026

Emerging Space Technologies

As India moves toward greater self-reliance and bolder goals, a new generation of technologies is taking shape to power this journey. These innovations span next-generation launch systems, in-space operations, human spaceflight, and advanced navigation and communications. They mark a shift from India’s early achievements to a future-ready space programme. Built for the decades ahead, these associated programmes aim to keep India competitive, connected and firmly self-reliant.

Next-Generation Launch Vehicles (NGLV)

Access to space begins with the ability to launch. A country that can build and fly its own rockets decides when, how and at what cost it reaches space. India’s launch journey has moved from small, single-use (expendable) rockets to heavy-lift vehicles, and it is now moving towards reusable systems.

India's Traditional Launch Vehicles

  • PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle): PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle), ISRO’s workhorse, can carry up to 1,750 kg to a 600-km Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit (SSPO) and up to 1,425 kg to Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO), depending on mission configuration.
  • GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle): It uses the indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage and can carry communication satellites of up to the 2-tonne class.
  • LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3) is India’s heavy-lift launch vehicle. It can carry communication satellites of the 4-tonne class to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO), and payloads of the 10-tonne class to Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
  • SSLV (Small Satellite Launch Vehicle): SSLV is a three-stage vehicle weighing ~120 tonnes at lift-off. It can launch satellites of up to the ~500-kg class into a 500-km planar orbit.

In September 2024, the Union Cabinet approved the development of the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV). The approved outlay of ₹8,240 crore covers development costs, three developmental flights, essential facilities, programme management and the launch campaign. Designed for a maximum capacity of 30 tonnes to Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the NGLV triples India's current launch payload capability compared to the 10-tonne LEO limit of the LVM3. In addition, a partially reusable NGLV variant with a 14-tonne LEO payload capability is being developed to support lower-cost access to space. Its reusability feature will also lower the cost of reaching space.

NGLV will enable both national and commercial missions. These include human spaceflight missions to the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, as well as lunar and interplanetary exploration. It will also launch communication and earth observation satellite constellations to Low Earth Orbit. These missions will benefit the entire space ecosystem and boost the nation’s capability and capacity.

Understanding Key Terms

Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO): A Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO) is a near-polar orbit in which a satellite passes over an area at approximately the same local solar time, enabling comparisons under similar illumination. The interval between repeat observations of a particular location varies with the satellite and its orbit.

Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO): GTO is an elliptical intermediate orbit used to transfer a satellite into geostationary orbit (GEO). Its lowest point (perigee) is typically a few hundred kilometres above Earth, while its highest point (apogee) is near 35,786 km above Earth's surface. The launch vehicle typically places the satellite in GTO rather than directly into GEO. Near apogee, the satellite fires its onboard apogee motor to raise its perigee and circularise the orbit. Additional manoeuvres may be required to align the orbit with Earth's equatorial plane. In GEO, the satellite orbits above the equator with a period matching Earth's rotation, appearing stationary relative to the ground.

Cryogenic Upper Stage: A cryogenic upper stage is the final stage of a launch vehicle that uses these propellants to provide the high efficiency needed to place satellites into their intended orbits. ISRO’s indigenous cryogenic upper stage used on GSLV employs liquid hydrogen (LH₂) as fuel and liquid oxygen (LOX) as oxidiser, both stored at extremely low temperatures. It replaced the Russian-supplied stage used in earlier GSLV flights, strengthening India’s self-reliance in advanced launch vehicle technology.

Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV)

RLV technologies can help reduce launch costs and improve operational efficiency. Unlike conventional expendable (single-use) launch vehicles, reusable systems are designed to recover major components for subsequent missions. Their development requires controlled atmospheric re-entry, autonomous navigation, aerodynamic flight and precision landing. ISRO has demonstrated autonomous runway-landing technologies using its winged Reusable Launch Vehicle technology demonstrator, Pushpak. The three RLV Landing Experiments were completed on 2 April 2023, 22 March 2024 and 23 June 2024, respectively. LEX-03 validated autonomous landing under more challenging cross-range and wind conditions.

Scramjet Technology: Powering India’s Reusable Space Transportation

A scramjet (supersonic combustion ramjet) is an air-breathing jet engine. It carries only fuel and draws oxygen from the surrounding air. Conventional rockets haul both fuel and oxidiser. A scramjet is therefore lighter and can deliver more payload for the same lift-off mass. It works only within the atmosphere at very high velocity, so a booster must first accelerate it. Its velocity is expressed as a Mach number. Mach 1 equals the speed of sound. Anything above Mach 5 is called hypersonic. Scramjets can complement reusable launch vehicles, which retrieve and refly major parts to cut costs. They offer a promising path to affordable space access. India flight-tested its scramjet in 28 August 2016. It reached Mach 6, a hypersonic velocity, making the country the fourth to demonstrate this. On 22 July 2024, ISRO separately conducted an experimental RH-560 sounding-rocket flight to demonstrate air-breathing propulsion systems and assess their performance.

 

Indigenous Space Hardware and Critical Technologies

Every space mission relies on critical technologies, including engines, thrusters, fuels and power systems. Developing these technologies within India helps reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and strengthens the country’s ability to build and operate spacecraft independently. ISRO is advancing indigenous propulsion technologies, including electric propulsion and alternative fuels. It is also exploring technologies for future missions. These efforts contribute to India’s long-term goal of self-reliance in space.

One important area of progress is electric propulsion, which uses electrical energy to accelerate propellant and generate thrust. Compared with conventional chemical propulsion, it can achieve the same orbital changes using much less propellant. This reduces the fuel carried by a satellite and frees up mass for communication equipment and other payloads. On 27 March 2025, ISRO successfully completed a 1,000-hour life test of its indigenous 300 mN stationary plasma thruster. Its specific impulse, a measure of propulsion efficiency, is at least six times that of conventional propulsion systems. ISRO plans to validate the technology aboard its Technology Demonstration Satellite (TDS-01). It is intended to support future electric-propulsion satellites, including orbit raising and station keeping.

Alongside electric propulsion, ISRO is developing alternative propellants to reduce environmental impacts and improve propulsion efficiency i.e., Green Propulsion. One example is ISROSENE, a rocket-grade kerosene. Liquid oxygen–kerosene propellants are being developed for semicryogenic rocket-engine applications.

Progress in green propulsion also extends beyond ISRO’s own development programmes. Under DRDO’s Technology Development Fund, Bengaluru-based Bellatrix Aerospace developed a 1 N-class green monopropellant thruster for microsatellite attitude control and orbit keeping. Its in-orbit functionality was demonstrated on a payload launched aboard PSLV-C58 in January 2024.

These developments illustrate India’s progress in indigenous electric and green propulsion technologies. Continued testing and validation will help determine their readiness for wider use in future space missions.

Radioisotope Heating and Power Technologies

ISRO and Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) are collaborating on requirements for Radioisotope Heater Units (RHU), which supply heat, and Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTG), which convert radioisotope heat into electrical power ISRO is collaborating with the DAE on RHU and RTG requirements for possible future Chandrayaan and Mars missions.

In-Space Operations and Human Spaceflight

In-space operations are the activities spacecraft carry out once they are in orbit, such as rendezvous, docking and undocking. Launching a satellite is only the first step: complex missions such as a space station, a crewed flight or a lunar sample return depend on what spacecraft can do after launch. In-space docking technology is essential when multiple rocket launches are needed to achieve common mission objectives, and it underpins ambitions such as sample return from the Moon and the building and operation of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station.

ISRO’s SpaDeX mission first docked its two satellites on 16 January 2025 and subsequently demonstrated undocking. A second docking was completed with full autonomy from an inter-satellite distance of 15 m on 20th April 2025. Bidirectional power transfer between the docked satellites was demonstrated on 21st April 2025. India thereby became the fourth country to demonstrate space docking, after the United States, Russia and China. This achievement also advances technologies required for future missions.

Beyond joining spacecraft, docking enables them to work together in orbit. In-orbit servicing could, in future, enable refuelling, repair or upgrading of spacecraft in orbit, without bringing them back to Earth. SpaDeX demonstrated docking, undocking and power transfer. These interventions can extend satellite lifespans and reduce the need for replacement missions. These achievements provide important technological building blocks for developing future in-orbit servicing capabilities.

Next-Generation Navigation and Communications

Satellite navigation and communication systems support essential services across India. Navigation satellites provide positioning, navigation and timing information, while communication satellites relay television, telephone, broadband and other data signals. Together, these systems support transportation, financial services, telecommunications, disaster management and national security. India is strengthening these capabilities through ISRO’s indigenous NavIC navigation system and communication satellites.

Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) is India’s independent regional satellite navigation system, developed and maintained by ISRO. It provides positioning, navigation and timing services across India and up to 1,500 kilometres beyond the Indian mainland. NavIC offers a Standard Positioning Service for civilian users and an encrypted Restricted Service for authorized users. These capabilities support terrestrial, aerial and maritime navigation, surveying, vehicle tracking and precise timing. NavIC also supports emergency warning messages for fishermen operating beyond terrestrial network coverage. Its integration into compatible devices and applications can further expand its use across civilian and strategic sectors.

Additionally, India’s communication satellites support broadcasting, broadband connectivity and secure communications. GSAT-24, launched aboard Ariane-5 from Kourou, French Guiana, on 23 June 2022 at 03:20 IST (22 June local time), was realised to meet Direct-to-Home (DTH) television requirements in India. Building on this capability, GSAT-N2 (GSAT-20) was launched on 19 November 2024. This high-throughput satellite has a capacity of approximately 48 Gbps and is designed to support broadband and in-flight connectivity across India, including remote island regions.

Communication satellites also serve India’s defence requirements. CMS-03, also known as GSAT-7R, was launched on 2 November 2025. It is a dedicated communication satellite for the Indian Navy. These satellites strengthen India's space-based communication infrastructure and support civilian connectivity, maritime operations and national security.

Advanced Earth Observation Satellites

Earth observation satellites monitor the land, oceans, ice-covered regions and atmosphere from space. Their data supports agriculture, disaster management, water resource planning, climate research and national security. Between December 2020 and December 2025, ISRO launched 22 satellites, including seven Earth observation satellites. These satellites provide images and data for monitoring natural resources, tracking environmental changes and supporting informed planning. India continues to strengthen these capabilities through advanced technologies, including radar imaging and hyperspectral observation.

A major advancement in Earth observation is the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission. It was launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 from Sriharikota. It is the first satellite mission to use two radar frequencies together: NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band. Radar can collect data through clouds and in darkness, enabling observations in almost all-weather conditions, both day and night. NISAR is designed to observe the Earth’s land and ice-covered surfaces every 12 days. Its data can help scientists monitor ground deformation, glacier movement, vegetation changes, soil moisture and natural hazards. These observations can also support coastal monitoring and disaster response.

While radar reveals changes in the Earth’s surface, hyperspectral imaging helps identify different materials and surface characteristics. ISRO launched the Hyperspectral Imaging Satellite (HysIS) on 29 November 2018. It observes the Earth’s surface in visible, near-infrared and shortwave-infrared wavelengths. By recording information across numerous narrow bands of light, HysIS can distinguish features that ordinary imaging may not readily identify. Its data supports applications in agriculture, forestry, soil and geological studies, coastal zones and inland waters.

Did You Know? HysIS was launched alongside 30 foreign satellites from eight countries. These comprised one micro-satellite and 29 nano-satellites. The participating countries were Australia, Canada, Colombia, Finland, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Spain and the United States. Of these, 23 satellites were from the United States. The launch also demonstrated PSLV’s capability to deploy multiple satellites for international customers.

 

Way Forward: Building a US$44 Billion Space Economy

India’s space sector is increasingly contributing to economic growth, private investment and industrial capability, alongside its scientific and strategic goals. As per the Department of Space, India’s space economy is targeted to reach US$44 billion by 2033. Emerging technologies such as reusable launch vehicles, air-breathing propulsion, electric propulsion and in-space docking are supporting this growth.

This technological momentum is already creating economic opportunity. NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) has signed 118 Technology Transfer Agreements to transfer 83 technologies developed by ISRO to Indian industry. As a result, investor confidence is also growing. Cumulative investment in Indian space start-ups reached approximately US$618.5 million as of 31 March 2026, with funding shifting from early-stage seed support to larger, growth-stage rounds.

Together, these developments show that India's emerging space technologies are not only advancing national capability but also building a strong, enterprise-led space economy for the years ahead.

2329321.title: Green Hydrogen
2329321.body_html:
PIB Backgrounder
Green Hydrogen
Emerging Pillar of India’s Clean Energy Transition
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 11:15AM by PIB Delhi

Green hydrogen is emerging as a pillar of India’s clean energy transition. It is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity. It can help reduce emissions in sectors such as fertiliser production, petroleum refining, iron and steel manufacturing, heavy-duty road transport and shipping. The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) supports domestic manufacturing, production, assured demand and credible certification. From green ammonia auctions to India’s first hydrogen train, early projects point to a promising path.

Why Green Hydrogen

Hydrogen is an energy carrier that stores energy and delivers it for varied uses. In a fuel cell, it reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, leaving only water and heat as by-products, and no polluting compounds or greenhouse gases. Although pure hydrogen is not found in large quantities in nature,  it can be extracted from compounds such as water or natural gas. Its environmental impact therefore depends on how it is made. Conventional methods rely on fossil fuels and release carbon emissions.

Production using renewable electricity from solar and wind power can cut this footprint substantially. Hydrogen made by splitting water using renewable power is called green hydrogen. Unlike fossil-based routes, this process emits far less carbon. India’s abundant solar and wind resources make domestic production feasible. This diversifies the country’s energy sources and strengthens energy security. It also supports India’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2070.

Green hydrogen matters most in sectors where cutting emissions is difficult. Reasons include high-temperature heat needs, chemical processes and few alternatives to fossil fuels. These hard-to-abate sectors include fertiliser, petroleum refining, iron and steel, heavy-duty road transport and shipping. Fertiliser and refining plants already use hydrogen, so green hydrogen can replace the fossil-based supply. It can also support lower-emission steelmaking, selected transport uses and energy storage. It is especially useful where direct electrification is difficult or less practical.

For India, wider adoption could reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. It would also lessen exposure to global fuel price swings. The sector could open opportunities in manufacturing, draw investment, create jobs and expand exports. Building capabilities across the value chain would strengthen domestic supply chains and spur industrial innovation. Green hydrogen can thus support self-reliance, sustainable industrial growth and a low-carbon future.

What Makes Hydrogen “Green”

Hydrogen releases no carbon dioxide when used, so its climate impact depends on how it is produced. In August 2023, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified India’s Green Hydrogen Standard. Hydrogen qualifies as green if emissions do not exceed 2 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, on a well-to-gate basis, measured as a 12-month average. India thus became one of the first few countries to define green hydrogen formally.

 

 

Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies

 

ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India’s Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave, is being held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Organised by the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), the conclave follows the theme “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.” It advances emerging frontiers in science and technology, including energy technologies such as Green Hydrogen Technology. Spanning 12 thematic areas, ESTIC-2026 features plenary sessions, technical discussions and exhibitions. The conclave also promotes strategic collaborations in support of India’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Read More on Agenda: ESTIC 2026

 

How Is Green Hydrogen Produced?

Green hydrogen is produced mainly through water (H₂O) electrolysis. Electrolysis uses electricity to split a compound into simpler substances. Here, renewable electricity splits water into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), with minimal emissions.

2H2O   →   2H2   +   O2

The key equipment is the electrolyser. It contains two electrodes, a cathode and an anode, connected to a power source. They operate within an electrolyte, which helps ions move through the cell. A diaphragm keeps the gases apart while allowing ions to pass. When current flows, hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The gases are collected separately for further usage. An electrolyser thus turns renewable electricity and water into a low-emission fuel for industry, transport and other uses.

Did You Know? Water is purified before electrolysis, because impurities can damage cells and shorten their life. According to MNRE, about nine litres of demineralised water is needed per kg of hydrogen. Afterwards, the hydrogen is dried and purified before compression. India’s Green Hydrogen Standard counts emissions from each of these steps.

 

Applications of Green Hydrogen

  • Fertilisers: Ammonia, made from hydrogen and nitrogen, is the base for nitrogen fertilisers such as urea. Most of this hydrogen now comes from natural gas. Green hydrogen can replace it and yield green ammonia with far lower emissions.
  • Petroleum refineries: Refineries use hydrogen to remove sulphur from petrol and diesel, so the fuels burn cleaner. They also use it to upgrade heavy oil into lighter fuels such as diesel, aviation turbine fuel and naphtha. These fuels serve road transport, aviation and industry. Most refinery hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, so a green supply can cut refining emissions.
  • Steel: Conventional steelmaking uses coal to strip oxygen from iron ore, releasing carbon dioxide. In direct reduced iron routes, green hydrogen can do this job instead. The reduction stage then releases water vapour in place of carbon dioxide.
  • City gas networks: Green hydrogen can be blended with natural gas in limited proportions, subject to safety standards and infrastructure compatibility. This allows existing gas networks to supply a hydrogen-natural gas blend to homes, businesses and industries. Such blending can reduce fossil fuel consumption and associated emissions while utilising existing distribution infrastructure.
  • Road and rail transport: Fuel-cell vehicles convert hydrogen into electricity on board, which drives electric motors. Their only emission at the point of use is water vapour. This suits buses, trucks and trains that need long range and quick refuelling.

Did You Know?

India’s first indigenous hydrogen-powered train was inaugurated on 17 July 2026 on the Jind–Sonipat section. The 10-car trainset can carry around 2,600 passengers. A facility at Jind stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen. The train emits only water vapour and heat. Click to Read More

 

  • Shipping: Green hydrogen can be converted into green ammonia and green methanol, which can fuel ships. These can replace conventional marine fuels on long voyages. Adoption depends on engine compatibility, safety requirements and port infrastructure.
  • Exports: India can supply green hydrogen and derivatives, such as green ammonia and green methanol, to countries seeking low-emission fuels. India’s renewable energy resources can support this supply. Exports can open industrial opportunities and strengthen India’s position in low-emission fuels. Bringing Cohesion in Government Approach

The Government has adopted an integrated strategy to increase the adoption of Green hydrogen across the sector. It coordinates with Central and State Ministries, Departments, agencies and institutions to drive adoption. Each Ministry has a defined role. For example, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas promotes use in refineries and city gas distribution; Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers encourage indigenous green ammonia-based fertilisers; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways enable transport use through regulations, standards and codes; Ministry of Steel drives adoption in steelmaking; Ministry of External Affairs facilitates collaboration with global partners.

India’s Green Hydrogen Policy Architecture

NGHM: A mission for the whole ecosystem

MNRE is implementing the NGHM to make India a global hub for green hydrogen and its derivatives. The Union Cabinet approved the Mission in January 2023 with an outlay of Rs19,744 crore. It targets production capacity of at least 5 million metric tonnes (MMT) annually by 2030. With export demand, this could reach 10 MMT per year. The Mission has the following components.

SIGHT: Support on both sides of the market

The Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) Programme is a key NGHM component. Its outlay is Rs17,490 crore up to 2029–30. It offers incentives for two purposes: domestic electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production. Together, they strengthen indigenous capability and speed up production.

Key Progress

  • Incentives have been awarded to 15 companies for 3,000 MW per annum of electrolyser manufacturing capacity. This reduces dependence on imported supply chains.
  • About 8,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen capacity had been commissioned by February 2026.
  • Incentives have been awarded for 8,62,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen production capacity.

 

Pilot Projects

The NGHM supports pilots that replace fossil fuels and feedstocks in hard-to-abate sectors. These include steel, heavy-duty mobility and shipping. The pilots aim to identify technological, regulatory and infrastructure gaps. They will also test supply chains and technology integration. Their findings will guide commercial-scale deployment and the policy support needed. The Mission has earmarked Rs455 crore for low-carbon steel up to 2029–30. It has also earmarked Rs496 crore for mobility and Rs115 crore for shipping up to 2025–26.

Key Progress

  • Five pilot projects have been sanctioned in the steel sector. Rs84 crore is sanctioned for testing 100% hydrogen injection.
  • Twelve projects will deploy 70 hydrogen vehicles: 27 buses and 43 trucks. These include fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and hydrogen internal combustion engine (H₂-ICE) vehicles.
  • The projects also cover 16 hydrogen refuelling stations across 21 routes. Financial assistance of Rs41.58 crore has been released.
  • V.O. Chidambaranar Port Authority has awarded a pilot project to develop bunkering and refuelling facilities for green methanol. The project costs Rs 38.12 crore, including an MNRE grant of Rs 35 crore.

 

Green Hydrogen Hubs and Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters (HVIC)

Hydrogen is difficult to transport. To address this, the Mission promotes hubs and HVICs. This cluster approach brings production, consumption and infrastructure together. It improves project viability and enables economies of scale. Projects in designated hubs can also access Central and State scheme benefits. The Mission has an outlay of Rs 400 crore up to 2025–26 for hubs and related projects. These initiatives aim to attract green investment and accelerate innovation.

Key Progress

  • MNRE has recognised Deendayal Port (Kandla, Gujarat), V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu) and Paradip Port (Odisha) as hubs.
  • An indigenously built 1 MW green hydrogen plant was commissioned at Kandla Port in July 2025.
  • Four HVICs have been awarded: Jodhpur, Odisha, Pune and Kerala.

 

Enabling Policy Framework

The Mission follows a whole-of-government approach to make green hydrogen affordable. MNRE coordinates with Central and State departments on benefits and project facilitation. Key measures include waiving interstate transmission charges and facilitating renewable energy banking. They also include time-bound Open Access and grid connectivity. The Government will coordinate planning for renewable capacity, transmission, banking and storage. Solar Parks, Manufacturing Zones and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) may be extended to hydrogen facilities. The Mission will also explore international green finance, green bonds and innovative financing.

Key Progress

  • Green hydrogen and green ammonia plants commissioned by 31 December 2030 are exempt from Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) charges for 25 years. ISTS are fees for moving power across state boundaries. The waiver lowers electricity costs.
  • The Green Energy Corridor Scheme supports lines and substations that carry renewable power to the grid. A national transmission plan improves links between generation and consumption centres. Click to Read More
  • Duty benefits under Section 26 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, have been extended to eligible units installing and operating renewable energy equipment exclusively for captive consumption. This can reduce the cost of setting up renewable energy facilities within SEZs to meet their own electricity requirements.
  • Standalone plants producing green hydrogen or green ammonia through water electrolysis using renewable energy have been exempted from prior Environmental Clearance under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006. This can simplify the approval process for eligible projects.
  • Renewable energy plants located within a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) or Export Oriented Unit (EOU) are exempt from the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) and Revised List of Models and Manufacturers (RLMM) requirements when supplying electricity exclusively to green hydrogen production plants or their derivatives. This provides eligible projects greater flexibility in sourcing renewable energy equipment, subject to the applicable exemption conditions.
  • The Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy provides for Open Access within 15 days and banking of surplus renewable electricity for up to 30 days, subject to applicable provisions. Open Access allows producers to procure renewable electricity from sources other than their local distribution company. Banking allows surplus electricity to be stored as a credit and used later, subject to applicable regulations.

 

Regulations and Standards

The Mission is building regulations and standards aligned with industry needs. The aim is to enable sector growth and harmonise with international norms.

Key Progress

  • India’s Green Hydrogen Standard has been notified. It sets a ceiling of 2 kg CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, well-to-gate, averaged over a 12-month period. This created a common benchmark.
  • Scheme guidelines have been issued to fund testing facilities, infrastructure and institutional support for standards.
  • Standards for green ammonia and green methanol have been notified. They set emission thresholds and eligibility conditions, supporting production and trade.
  • MNRE launched the Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India in April 2025. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) accredits agencies for monitoring, verification and certification.
  • A dedicated portal went live in June 2026 for transparent certification and compliance. Credible certification will help Indian producers compete with confidence globally.

Research and Development

The Mission supports research and development (R&D) to make green hydrogen more affordable, efficient, safe and reliable. The Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership (SHIP) is a public-private framework, with a dedicated R&D fund from industry and Government. Scheme guidelines for R&D were notified in March 2024, with an outlay of Rs 400 crore. As of June 2026, an initial R&D roadmap worth Rs 113 crore is supporting approved projects across hydrogen production, storage, and safety technologies.

Skilling

A coordinated skill development initiative is under way. The Mission aims to generate over 6 lakh jobs across the value chain by 2030. So far, 8,149 candidates have been trained and 7,248 certified in hydrogen-related qualifications across 14 States and Union Territories. Training spans renewable power for electrolysers, electrolysis, storage, transport, safety standards and end use such as steel, mobility and refining. For innovation, Rs 100 crore has been allocated to start-ups working on green hydrogen technologies. The first nine start-ups have been approved, with total funding of Rs22 crore.

 

International Cooperation

The Mission promotes partnerships to develop technology, mobilise investment, build export markets and align standards.

Key Progress

  • MNRE, directly or through the National Institute of Solar Energy, has signed MoUs, Letters of Intent or Joint Declarations of Intent. The partners are Australia, Finland, France, Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Uzbekistan.
  • An MoU on renewable energy has been signed with the Netherlands.
  • An India–US Hydrogen Task Force has been formed under the Strategic Clean Energy Partnership.
  • Green hydrogen is a focus area of the India–US New and Emerging Renewable Energy Technology Action Platform (RETAP).

 

State-level Initiatives

Six States have notified dedicated green hydrogen policies, complementing the National Green Hydrogen Mission. Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal are the States with notified dedicated policies.

Four more States are finalising their dedicated green hydrogen policies. Haryana, Punjab, Bihar and Keralam are working on the draft policies.

Seven States have integrated hydrogen into their existing industrial and renewable energy policy frameworks. These include Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana and Chhattisgarh.

The Road Ahead

The National Green Hydrogen Mission marks an important step towards building a cleaner, more self-reliant and globally competitive energy economy. By 2030, India aims to develop 5 million metric tonnes (MMT) of annual green hydrogen production capacity. This transition can reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the country’s long-term energy security. The Mission is expected to reduce cumulative fossil fuel imports by approximately Rs1 lakh crore by 2030.

Beyond energy security, the Mission seeks to create new opportunities for industrial growth, investment and employment. It is expected to mobilise over Rs8 lakh crore in investments and generate more than 6 lakh jobs across manufacturing, infrastructure, research and project development. The production and use of the targeted green hydrogen quantum could also help avert nearly 50 MMT of carbon dioxide emissions annually. Through these efforts, the Government aims to accelerate industrial decarbonisation, strengthen domestic manufacturing and position India as a global hub for green hydrogen production, use and exports. This will contribute to India’s broader vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047 and its commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.

2329318.title: DRI seizes around 55,000 e-cigarettes worth more than Rs. 13.5 crore in two operations at Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port in Kolkata
2329318.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
DRI seizes around 55,000 e-cigarettes worth more than Rs. 13.5 crore in two operations at Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port in Kolkata
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 11:04AM by PIB Delhi

The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) continues its sustained crackdown on illicit trade and seized over 55,000 smuggled e-cigarettes at Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, on 24th October 2026.

Acting on specific intelligence DRI officers intercepted two containers Nepal-bound transshipment consignment suspected to contain e-cigarettes. The goods had been mis-declared as “water glass” and “ceramic mugs” in another. A detailed examination of the first container led to the recovery of 40,000 pieces of e-cigarettes of brand IGET in various flavours, hidden among the declared cargo. Whereas, detailed examination of second container led to the recovery of around 15,000 pieces of e-cigarettes of various brands, including VTV, VOKO, Bang and Ejoy, hidden among the declared cargo.

In total around 55,000 e-cigarettes valued at Rs 13.50 crore were seized along with the cover cargo under relevant sections of Customs Act.

Electronic cigarettes and all Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems (ENDS) are prohibited in India under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes (Production, Manufacture, Import, Export, Transport, Sale, Distribution, Storage and Advertisement) Act, 2019, enacted in the interest of public health and to protect people from harm.

In the current FY 2026-27, DRI have already made seizure of around 3,00,000 e-cigarettes worth more than Rs. 120 crore in across various ports, airports, and ICDs in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Delhi and West Bengal.

2329316.title: DRI busts wildlife smuggling racket at Trichy Airport; 45 live reptiles recovered; 2 arrested
2329316.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
DRI busts wildlife smuggling racket at Trichy Airport; 45 live reptiles recovered; 2 arrested
Intelligence-led operation in coordination with Trichy Airport Customs seizes sedated reptiles concealed in food packets carried by passengers arriving from Bangkok via Colombo
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 11:03AM by PIB Delhi

The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), in a coordinated operation with the Air Intelligence Unit (AIU), Trichy, has foiled an attempt to smuggle 45 live reptiles into India through Trichy International Airport. Acting on specific intelligence, officers of DRI intercepted two Indian passengers arriving from Bangkok via Colombo on 26 October 2026. A systematic examination of their baggage led to the recovery of live wildlife concealed in 27 food packets, with the animals found in a sedated condition.

The recovered reptiles comprised 23 Corn Snakes, 16 Ball Pythons, 5 Argentine Black and White Tegus and 1 Snow White Iguana. The reptiles were seized, and the two passengers were arrested by AIU, Trichy, under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. The wildlife was recovered during the examination of the passengers’ baggage and handed over to AIU, Trichy, for further necessary action.

This successful interception underscores DRI’s commitment to combating wildlife trafficking through intelligence-led enforcement and close coordination with Customs authorities to prevent the illegal movement of wildlife into the country.

2329303.title: India and Mexico launch Negotiations for Preferential Trade Agreement, Sign Terms of Reference
2329303.body_html:
Ministry of Commerce & Industry
India and Mexico launch Negotiations for Preferential Trade Agreement, Sign Terms of Reference
India and Mexico Discuss Expanding Trade and Investment Ties; PTA Negotiations Cover Key Trade Areas
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 10:38AM by PIB Delhi

Mexico and India take an important step towards strengthening their economic and trade relations with the signing of the Terms of Reference for negotiations on a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA), which establish the framework, scope, modalities and roadmap for negotiations aimed at creating new economic opportunities for both countries.

The signing formally launches negotiations for a mutually beneficial and balanced PTA, with the potential to expand bilateral trade, create business opportunities, enhance investment flows and contribute to resilient and diversified supply chains.

The initiative follows the understanding reached between Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and President Dr. Claudia Sheinbaum during their meeting on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Canada in June 2025, when the two leaders agreed to further strengthen and deepen the India-Mexico partnership.

During the visit of Commerce Secretary, Shri Rajesh Agrawal, both delegations discussed bilateral relations and opportunities to expand trade and investment flows. The discussions were held with Mexico’s Undersecretary of Foreign Trade, Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano, who participated on behalf of Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard Casaubon.

The Terms of Reference cover key negotiating areas, including market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies.

The proposed agreement seeks to leverage the complementarities between the two economies and expand opportunities for Mexican products and businesses in the Indian market. With its strong linkages to global value chains, Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors. Sectors with significant potential for cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices and advanced manufacturing, among others.

The delegations also discussed various aspects of the bilateral economic agenda, identifying opportunities to deepen trade and investment relations, strengthen cooperation and foster closer ties between the productive sectors of both countries.

Both sides further discussed the possibility of organising a Mexican business mission to India during the first quarter of 2027. The proposed mission would facilitate business-to-business meetings, help identify commercial opportunities and strengthen commercial ties between the productive sectors of the two countries.

***

2329291.title: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurates Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026
2329291.body_html:
Ministry of Science & Technology
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi inaugurates Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave 2026
Called on the scientific community, researchers and young innovators to deliver concrete, measurable and scalable technological outcomes
Dr. Jitendra Singh highlights India’s rise as a global co-creator in science and technology and calls for stronger biotechnology capabilities
Prof. Ajay K. Sood calls for closer alignment of research, industry and policy across ESTIC’s 12 priority domains
Nobel Laureates Joachim Frank and Richard Roberts address advances in structural biology and life sciences at ESTIC 2026
Parallel sessions deliberate on advanced manufacturing, generative and autonomous AI, and system and synthetic biology
ESTIC 2026 brings research, industry and policy leaders together to advance science-led innovation
Posted On: 28 OCT 2026 10:01AM by PIB Delhi

The inaugural day of the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC) 2026 brought together more than 5,000 global delegates, including scientific leaders, policymakers and deep-tech startups, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on October 27. The day’s programme combined addresses by national science and technology leaders, two Nobel Laureate plenary talks, three parallel technical sessions, a startup exhibition and poster track, an evening panel discussion along with the inaugural session. Across these proceedings, the focus was on connecting foundational research with industrial scale-up, public purpose and the development of technologies that can strengthen India’s capabilities and contribute to global welfare.

In his inaugural address, Prime Minister Sri Narendra Modi called on the scientific community, researchers and young innovators to deliver concrete, measurable and scalable technological outcomes within a three-year operational horizon. He emphasised that scientific breakthroughs should move beyond laboratory settings to address real-world problems, reinforce national self-reliance under the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat, and advance human welfare. The address also reaffirmed India’s commitment to setting global benchmarks in frontier areas, including artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, advanced materials and biotechnology.

Dr. Jitendra Singh, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences, described a shift in India’s role in science and technology, from being a consumer of technologies to becoming a future-ready global co-creator of frontier scientific solutions. He highlighted the expansion of the country’s startup ecosystem from approximately 400 startups in 2014 to more than 2.3 lakh today. An estimated 50 to 60 per cent of these startups are based in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, the Minister cited as evidence of the wider spread of technological entrepreneurship.

Dr. Jitendra Singh also identified India’s genetic and phenotypic diversity as an important resource for biotechnology and called for stronger domestic capabilities in gene synthesis, systems biology and nuclear medicine. He referred to recent legislative reforms, including the SHANTI Act, in the context of accelerating work in these fields. His remarks placed indigenous research capability and the development of applications from India’s scientific strengths among the priorities for the country’s biotechnology ecosystem.

Prof. Ajay K. Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, set out the need for closer alignment between basic scientific research, industrial scale-up and regulatory policy. He described ESTIC’s 12 core thematic priority domains and identified areas including quantum communication, generative and autonomous artificial intelligence, semiconductor fabrication, advanced manufacturing and the Deep Ocean Mission. His address situated the conclave as a forum for connecting research with the institutions, industrial capacities and policy frameworks needed to develop sovereign national capabilities.

Prof. Joachim Frank of Columbia University, the 2017 Nobel Laureate in Chemistry, delivered a plenary talk on cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) in target discovery and drug design. His presentation covered computational and mathematical frameworks used in high-resolution, single-particle Cryo-EM and the three-dimensional visualisation of macromolecular complexes. The session described how structural information about these complexes can support rational drug-design workflows and help researchers investigate biological targets.

Sir Richard J. Roberts, the 1993 Nobel Laureate in Physiology or Medicine, delivered a separate plenary on split genes and frontiers in life sciences. His talk covered the fundamental mechanisms of gene splicing, microbial genomics and restriction-modification enzymes. It also considered biotechnology initiatives relevant to sustainable agriculture, public health and diagnostics, linking advances in the life sciences with applications in food systems and healthcare.

Earlier, Dr. Jitendra Singh inaugurated the startup exhibition and poster track. The exhibition featured deep-tech research and development displays, startup prototype showcases and interactive poster presentations. It provided an opportunity for industry stakeholders, investors, academic researchers and policymakers to engage with research and emerging technologies across the conclave’s areas of focus.

The Advanced Manufacturing session, chaired by Dr. (Mrs.) N. Kalaiselvi, Director General of CSIR, featured a keynote address by Dr. G. Satheesh Reddy, former Chairman of the Defence Research and Development Organisation. The listed speakers included Shri Rajat Verma, Ms. Chaya Nanjappa, Dr. N. C. Murmu, Dr. C. Anandharamakrishnan and Dr. Nagahanumaiah. The session focused on implementing digital twins, collaborative robots, additive manufacturing and metrology, and on strengthening supply chains for micro, small and medium enterprises. These areas framed the discussion on how advanced manufacturing capabilities can connect research and engineering with industrial production and strengthen the domestic manufacturing base.

The Generative and Autonomous AI session was chaired by Shri Saurabh Vijay, Chief Executive Officer of IndiaAI, and featured a keynote address by Prof. Mitesh M. Khapra of IIT Madras. The session saw the participation of Prof. Chetan Arora, Dr. Alpan Raval, Prof. Balaraman Ravindran and Shri S. Krishnan, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, among the key speakers. Discussion areas included the development of homegrown large language models, access to high-performance computing under IndiaAI, agentic artificial intelligence and frameworks for safe deployment. The session addressed the development of domestic AI capabilities and the conditions needed for responsible deployment of these technologies.

The System and Synthetic Biology session focused on engineered biological systems and the BioE3 national strategy. Its central framework was the “Understand, Design, Build, Test, Learn” cycle for biological design. The session identified precision biotherapeutics, metabolic pathway design, biofortified crops and waste-to-value biomanufacturing as areas of application. Together, these themes presented synthetic biology as a route from understanding biological systems to designing and testing them for applications in health, agriculture and manufacturing.

The evening panel discussion, “Science and Disruptive Technologies for Atmanirbhar Bharat,” was chaired by Prof. Ajay K. Sood. The listed panellists were Dr. Tessy Thomas, Gen. N. S. Raja Subramani, Prof. Bhanu P. Jena, Dr. Samir Saran and Prof. V. K. Singh. The discussion addressed defence technological sovereignty, commercialisation of intellectual property, deep-tech funding and mechanisms for technology transfer across sectors. These themes brought together questions of research translation, strategic capability and the movement of technologies between research institutions and industry.

ESTIC 2026 is organised around 12 thematic priority domains and brings together researchers, government, industry and startups. The Day 1 proceedings linked foundational science with practical work in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence and engineered biological systems, while the plenary sessions addressed developments in structural biology and the life sciences. The Day -1 sessions identified the ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Fund and ANRF mechanisms as avenues for advancing deep-tech development through technology-readiness stages towards commercialised products. The conclave’s stated purpose is to strengthen the connections that enable science and technology to contribute to national development and wider human welfare.
